doc.title: Plas Johnson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996

title: Radio music and early saxophone heroes in New Orleans
summary: Dixieland and blues on the radio, his father's Ellington and Hodges records, Louis Jordan and bebop players; the importance of disc jockeys choosing their music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: What kind of music was popular on the radio when you were forming your musical—

In New Orleans it was Dixieland music and blues music. Great blues music. I’ll say blues music it included artists like Dinah Washington, you know she sang blues but you know she was just a great singer. And I heard Louis Jordan and well all blues artists, T-Bone Walker, B.B. King. My father was an Ellington fan so we had some Ellington records and he was also a Johnny Hodges fan, he was an alto player so his great thrill in life would have been to play like Johnny Hodges, which of course he couldn’t do.
Not many people could. Yeah, he had a sound. How about saxophone players that caught your attention in the beginning?

In the beginning? The blues players. Louis Jordan, hard swinging blues player. Later on in the middle ‘40s I guess I heard some of the bebop players or players that were on the bebop label like Don Byas and that. Let’s see, Gene Ammons was popular on the radio too. So it was kind of a combination of all kinds of music and you know, D.J.s in those days they got to, some of them got to select what they wanted to play instead of maybe like today where a program director does that and the D.J. just makes conversation
between the takes a lot of times. I think very few D.J.s now get to select their own programming.
Yeah. Jimmy Witherspoon was talking about that earlier, about how important the D.J.s were. Each city had its own kind of personality.
Right. So they played what they liked and if a D.J., he would get a following by what he played, if people liked what he played then they would tune in to his program.
